title: Ibbetson, Natural Law in Early Modern Legal Thought

1.title: Two roots and one channel
1.text: The whole article can be reduced to a single line, and it is worth being able to recite it. Modern natural law thinking has TWO MAIN ROOTS: GRAECO-ROMAN MORAL PHILOSOPHY, especially ARISTOTLE AND THE STOICS, and the ROMAN LAW of the late and post-classical period. These two sources came together IN 16TH-CENTURY SPAIN, especially at the UNIVERSITY OF SALAMANCA, from where they were taken over by the Dutchman HUGO GROTIUS. GROTIUS IS THE CHANNEL THROUGH WHICH THAT THINKING REACHED A EUROPE-WIDE AUDIENCE — his work and that of his followers then had an enormous influence on legal thought and practice after the 17th century. What changed in the process: NATURAL LAW CEASED TO BE REGARDED AS DEPENDENT ON THE WILL OF GOD; from self-evident premises a RATIONAL STRUCTURE could be derived, and the discovery of the concrete rules of natural law was regarded as THE WORK OF HUMAN REASON. It was precisely these features, together with an APPARENT MORAL OBJECTIVITY, that allowed natural law to serve as a MODEL FOR POSITIVE LEGAL ORDERS — and drove the movement towards CODIFICATION in 18th-century Europe.

cards.q: What are the two roots of modern natural law, and who is the main channel of its diffusion?
cards.a: Graeco-Roman moral philosophy (Aristotle, the Stoics) and the Roman law of the late and post-classical period. They came together in 16th-century Spain, especially at SALAMANCA, and from there were taken over by HUGO GROTIUS — the channel through which they reached a Europe-wide audience.

cards.q: How does modern natural law differ from the older kind, and why did that lead to codifications?
cards.a: It ceased to depend on THE WILL OF GOD, a RATIONAL STRUCTURE was derived from self-evident premises, and the concrete rules were regarded as the work of HUMAN REASON. That, together with an apparent moral objectivity, allowed it to serve as a MODEL for positive legal orders — hence the codification movement of the 18th century.

2.title: Aristotle: just by nature and just by convention
2.text: Aristotle's ethics DOES NOT SET APART any area that could be called natural law, but THERE IS IN IT A CLEAR, IF LOOSELY FORMULATED, DIVISION between what is just BY NATURE and what is just BY CONVENTION. What is just by convention CHANGES FROM PLACE TO PLACE AND FROM TIME TO TIME; what is just by nature, being unchangeable, does not. And Aristotle's refinement, worth holding on to: NATURAL THINGS MAY BE AS THEY ARE BY NATURE AND YET BE CAPABLE OF BEING OTHERWISE — as when all men are naturally right-handed, but it might happen that all were ambidextrous. Natural here therefore does not mean necessary.

cards.q: How does Aristotle divide the just, and what does his example of right-handedness mean?
cards.a: Into just BY NATURE and just BY CONVENTION; what is just by convention changes from place to place and time to time, what is just by nature does not. The example of right-handedness shows that natural DOES NOT MEAN NECESSARY: things may be as they are by nature and yet be capable of being otherwise.

3.title: Cicero: five marks of the true law and two problems
3.text: The Stoics built on this, and Cicero's conception, as recorded by Lactantius in the 3rd century, contains all the elements of later thought: 'TRUE LAW IS RIGHT REASON IN AGREEMENT WITH NATURE, DIFFUSED AMONG ALL MEN; CONSTANT AND UNCHANGING… IT IS A SIN TO TRY TO ALTER THIS LAW, NOR IS IT ALLOWABLE TO ATTEMPT TO REPEAL ANY PART OF IT, AND IT IS IMPOSSIBLE TO ABOLISH IT ENTIRELY; NOR CAN WE BE RELEASED FROM ITS OBLIGATIONS BY SENATE OR PEOPLE; NOR DO WE NEED ANYONE TO EXPOUND OR INTERPRET IT; NOR WILL THERE BE ONE LAW AT ROME AND ANOTHER AT ATHENS, NOR ONE NOW AND ANOTHER TOMORROW, BUT ONE AND THE SAME LAW, ETERNAL AND UNCHANGEABLE, WILL BIND ALL PEOPLES AND ALL AGES.' FIVE MARKS: it is COMMON TO ALL MEN and not tied to place (unconventional in Aristotle's sense); MEN RECOGNISE IT AS IN AGREEMENT WITH 'RIGHT REASON' AND IT NEEDS NO INTERPRETATION; it is IMPLANTED IN NATURE; it is UNCHANGING IN TIME AND PLACE; and it is FUNDAMENTAL in the sense that it cannot properly be altered nor can one be released from it. And TWO PROBLEMS which a millennium then worked on: THERE IS NO ATTEMPT TO IDENTIFY THE SOURCE of that true law (only that it agrees with nature), and the true law is SIMPLY POSITED — THE STATUS OF HUMAN LAWS THAT ACTUALLY COLLIDE WITH IT IS NOT EXAMINED.

cards.q: List the five marks of Cicero's 'true law'.
cards.a: It is common to all men and not tied to place; men recognise it as in agreement with 'right reason' and it needs no interpretation; it is implanted in nature; it is unchanging in time and place; and it is fundamental — it cannot properly be altered nor can one be released from it by senate or popular assembly.

cards.q: Which two problems does Cicero's conception leave open?
cards.a: It does not identify the SOURCE of the true law — only that it agrees with nature. And it simply POSITS the true law (or rather justice) without examining the status of human laws that actually collide with it. Both were worked on for the following millennium.

4.title: Roman law: a trichotomy without weight
4.text: Although some early Roman jurists such as QUINTUS MUCIUS SCAEVOLA were under Stoic influence, THERE IS NO TRACE OF NATURAL LAW IN THE WRITINGS OF THE REPUBLIC. Then and in the early empire the basic division was between IUS CIVILE — the law applying to Romans, or the law of any state — and IUS GENTIUM, those laws or institutions which were AS AN OBSERVABLE FACT COMMON TO EVERY STATE, such as SLAVERY or the CONTRACT OF SALE. The great jurists around AD 200 added elements of natural law, apparently under Stoic influence: in ULPIAN the trichotomy IUS CIVILE — IUS GENTIUM — IUS NATURALE emerges, with SLAVERY placed under ius gentium although UNDER NATURAL LAW ALL MEN ARE BORN FREE. Ius naturale is 'THAT WHICH NATURE HAS TAUGHT ALL ANIMALS'; in PAUL, 'THAT WHICH IS ALWAYS JUST AND EQUITABLE'. And now the essential assessment: NONE OF THESE IDEAS HAD ANY JURISPRUDENTIAL WEIGHT — they say little more than that there are principles of justice independent of the law. Post-classical law added CHRISTIANISATION without changing the Stoic core: JUSTINIAN'S INSTITUTES define natural rights as those 'WHICH ALL NATIONS OBSERVE ALIKE AND WHICH ARE AS IT WERE ESTABLISHED BY DIVINE PROVIDENCE; THEY REMAIN FIRM AND UNCHANGEABLE FOR EVER'. The introduction of God the creator made it possible to identify the SOURCE — but natural law still had no clear function BEYOND AN ELEGANT JUSTIFICATION OF SOME RULES OF POSITIVE LAW.

terms.term: ius civile – ius gentium – ius naturale
terms.def: Ulpian's trichotomy: civil law, the law of nations (what is in fact common to all states) and natural law — 'that which nature has taught all animals'.

cards.q: Explain Ulpian's trichotomy and what it does with slavery.
cards.a: Ius civile (the law of the Romans, or of any state), ius gentium (what is as an observable fact common to all states) and ius naturale ('that which nature has taught all animals'). Slavery is placed under IUS GENTIUM although under natural law all are born free — natural law therefore does not here override the positive rule.

cards.q: What legal weight did natural law have for the Roman jurists?
cards.a: None of its own. The ideas say little more than that there are principles of justice independent of the law, and even after Christianisation in Justinian — where the introduction of God the creator finally supplied a SOURCE — natural law has no function beyond an ELEGANT JUSTIFICATION of some rules of positive law.

5.title: Aquinas: three roads to the eternal law
5.text: The core of Thomas's concept of law is essentially POSITIVIST: law is 'AN ORDINANCE OF REASON FOR THE COMMON GOOD, MADE BY HIM WHO HAS CARE OF THE COMMUNITY, AND PROMULGATED'. But mankind is created and ultimately governed by God, who has no superior, so that the true law — the ETERNAL LAW — is the one laid down by God, unchanging in time and space. MAN CANNOT KNOW IT DIRECTLY, but it can be discovered in THREE WAYS. First, by DIVINE REVELATION through Scripture, whose authority is unquestionable — this is the DIVINE LAW. Second: SOME OF THE COMMANDS OF THE ETERNAL LAW ARE IMPRINTED IN MEN and every thinking person recognises them as self-evident — this is the NATURAL LAW. Third, the HUMAN LAW, the rules laid down by the ruler in a political community, whose authority as true law follows from the assumption that THE RULER EXERCISES HIS POWER BY DIVINE RIGHT.

terms.def: The eternal law laid down by God; man knows it not directly but through the divine law (revelation), the natural law (imprinted reason) and the human law.

cards.q: How does Aquinas define law, and in what three ways is the eternal law known?
cards.a: Law is 'an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by him who has care of the community, and promulgated' — a core essentially positivist. The eternal law is known by DIVINE REVELATION (divine law), by IMPRINTING in men, recognisable as self-evident (natural law), and by the rules of a RULER whose authority derives from exercising power by divine right (human law).

6.title: Aquinas: what to do when laws conflict
6.text: It can reasonably be assumed that human law will not contradict divine law, and if it did, THE DIVINE WOULD AUTOMATICALLY PREVAIL. A conflict between human and natural law cannot, however, be ruled out — although ADDING to natural law (fixing the measure of a penalty, say) is unproblematic. In such a case, according to Aquinas, THE NATURAL LAW PREVAILS, but WITH AN IMPORTANT QUALIFICATION: THE INDIVIDUAL SUBJECT SHOULD PERHAPS OBEY THE HUMAN LAW IF THIS IS NECESSARY 'TO AVOID SCANDAL AND DISTURBANCE'. From this follows a conclusion easily garbled in an exam: NATURAL LAW IN AQUINAS SERVES TO TEST THE VALIDITY OF HUMAN LAW WITHOUT IT NECESSARILY FOLLOWING THAT THE INDIVIDUAL MUST ALWAYS FOLLOW THE NATURAL LAW — THAT IS, HIS CONSCIENCE — AGAINST CONFLICTING POSITIVE LAW. And his treatment of IUS, that is of 'legal quality' or of right in the subjective sense, is different: LEX IS NOT ITSELF IUS, but is its foundation (RATIO IURIS), and its application is JUSTICE. Here there is a simple division of IUS NATURALE and IUS POSITIVUM: all laws, human and divine, take their 'legal quality' from one of the two.

cards.q: What does Aquinas hold in a conflict between human and natural law?
cards.a: The natural law prevails — but with the qualification that the individual subject should perhaps obey the human law if this is necessary 'to avoid scandal and disturbance'. Natural law therefore TESTS THE VALIDITY of human law without it necessarily following that the individual must always follow his conscience against positive law.

cards.q: What is the relation of lex and ius in Aquinas?
cards.a: Lex is NOT itself ius, but is its foundation (ratio iuris), and its application is JUSTICE. For ius there is then a simple division into ius naturale and ius positivum: all laws, human and divine, take their 'legal quality' from one of the two.

7.title: Salamanca: detachment from God in three steps
7.text: Watch how in the 16th century natural law detaches itself step by step from the divine command. DOMINGO DE SOTO, a Dominican, was the first to write a treatise DE JUSTITIA ET JURE. His shift is TERMINOLOGICAL AND THEREBY SUBSTANTIVE: whereas Aquinas asked whether the commands of the Old Testament are founded in natural law, SOTO EXPRESSLY SAYS THAT THE QUESTION IS NOT ONLY THAT, BUT WHETHER ALL MORAL PRECEPTS FOUNDED IN CUSTOM (MORES) COME FROM NATURAL LAW; and there is a SLIDE FROM LEX NATURALIS TO IUS NATURALE, that is a move towards EQUATING NATURAL LAW WITH MORAL PRINCIPLES. Soto nevertheless stresses that ALL LAW FLOWS FROM THE ETERNAL LAW, LEX LEGUM — the whole structure of his ius naturale thus hangs on the LEX AETERNA. Step two: the Jesuit LUIS DE MOLINA begins not with an exposition of LEX but directly of IUS and IUSTITIA, and does NOT EXPRESSLY CONNECT natural law with God — it is said to reside 'IN THE NATURE OF THE THING' (NATURA REI). Step three: a few decades later LEONARD LESSIUS likewise founds it in natura rei, and in HIM IT IS ALREADY EXPLICIT THAT IT DOES NOT DEPEND ON ANY DIVINE COMMAND. With that he is essentially back at Aristotle and the Stoics as reflected in Roman law.

terms.def: 'The nature of the thing' as the foundation of natural law in Molina and Lessius — in Lessius already expressly without dependence on a divine command.

cards.q: Describe the three steps by which natural law at Salamanca detached itself from God.
cards.a: SOTO still founds the whole ius naturale on the LEX AETERNA, but shifts the question from the commands of the Old Testament to whether all moral precepts founded in custom come from natural law, and slides from lex naturalis to ius naturale. MOLINA does not expressly connect natural law with God and places it in NATURA REI. LESSIUS then says expressly that it DOES NOT DEPEND ON ANY DIVINE COMMAND.

8.title: Grotius: it would hold even if God did not exist
8.text: Grotius was a Protestant but in De Jure Belli ac Pacis strongly influenced by the Spanish authors — evident especially from the second edition, whose notes refer to them expressly. He characterised natural law as A CORE OF UNCHANGING PRINCIPLES ARISING FROM NATURE IN SUCH A WAY THAT WE MIGHT RIGHTLY CONCLUDE THAT GOD HAD LAID THEM DOWN. BUT — and this is the famous sentence — HE AT ONCE ADDS THAT THEIR VALIDITY DOES NOT DEPEND ON GOD, SO THAT EVEN IF GOD DID NOT EXIST THEIR VALIDITY WOULD NOT BE AFFECTED IN ANY WAY. The best criterion of the truth of a proposition was for him AGREEMENT WITH WHAT MEN GENERALLY HOLD TO BE TRUE. He distinguished NATURAL LAW, derivable from first principles which are almost self-evident, and THE LAW OF NATIONS, which is NOT so derivable. And the core of natural law he found in the fact that MAN IS A SOCIAL ANIMAL AND DOES NOT SIMPLY PURSUE HIS OWN INTEREST: 'THE VERY NATURE OF MAN, WHICH WOULD LEAD US INTO THE MUTUAL RELATIONS OF SOCIETY EVEN IF WE LACKED NOTHING, IS THE MOTHER OF NATURAL LAW.'

terms.def: Grotius's thesis that natural law would hold even if God did not exist — hence its non-confessional form and Europe-wide reach.

cards.q: What does Grotius say about the relation of natural law and God?
cards.a: That they are unchanging principles arising from nature in such a way that we might rightly conclude God had laid them down — BUT their VALIDITY DOES NOT DEPEND ON GOD, so that even if God did not exist it would not be affected. The criterion of truth is agreement with what men generally hold to be true.

cards.q: Where does Grotius locate the core of natural law?
cards.a: In the fact that man is a SOCIAL ANIMAL and does not simply pursue his own interest: 'The very nature of man, which would lead us into the mutual relations of society even if we lacked nothing, is the mother of natural law.'

9.title: What Grotius derived from it — and where he was really new
9.text: From this starting point he derived the basic rules governing relations between states, reflecting Roman law a good deal: WE ARE TO ABSTAIN FROM TAKING WHAT BELONGS TO ANOTHER; WE ARE TO RESTORE TO THE OWNER ANOTHER'S PROPERTY THAT WE HOLD; WE ARE TO KEEP PROMISES; WE ARE TO MAKE GOOD THE DAMAGE WE HAVE CAUSED; PENALTIES ARE TO BE IMPOSED ACCORDING TO THE OFFENDER'S DESERT. He proceeded similarly twenty years earlier in DE IURE PRAEDAE ('The Law of Prize'), where he started from the propositions that IT IS PERMITTED TO DEFEND ONE'S LIFE AND AVOID WHAT IS HARMFUL and that IT IS PERMITTED TO ACQUIRE WHATEVER IS USEFUL FOR LIFE — deriving from them, among other things, that THE DUTCH HAVE A RIGHT TO FREE TRADE ACROSS THE SEAS. And now the sober assessment, which is worth more in an exam than a eulogy: as regards the IDEA of natural law itself, GROTIUS ADDED VERY LITTLE TO WHAT THE SCHOLASTICS OF THE PREVIOUS GENERATION HAD DONE, AND NOTHING AT ALL TO WHAT THE LATIN STOICS HAD WRITTEN. His importance lay in GIVING THE RULES OF NATURAL LAW A CONCRETE SHAPE, IN A NON-CONFESSIONAL FORM AND AT A DIGESTIBLE LENGTH. And his method was SEDUCTIVE: it appeared to derive concrete conclusions by pure rational procedure from premises any reader would accept.

cards.q: Where was Grotius really new, and where was he not?
cards.a: To the IDEA of natural law itself he added very little compared with the scholastics of the previous generation and nothing at all compared with the Latin Stoics. He was new in giving the rules a CONCRETE SHAPE, in a NON-CONFESSIONAL form and at a DIGESTIBLE length — and in a seductive method that appeared to derive concrete conclusions from premises acceptable to every reader.

cards.q: What basic rules did Grotius derive from man's sociability?
cards.a: To abstain from taking what belongs to another; to restore another's property we hold; to keep promises; to make good the damage we have caused; to impose penalties according to desert. From these he derived more concrete propositions — in De Iure Praedae he reached in this way the Dutch right to free trade across the seas.

10.title: Pufendorf: natural law as mathematics
10.text: After Grotius, secular natural law thinking gained respect: IN 1665 THE UNIVERSITY OF KIEL FILLED THE FIRST EUROPEAN CHAIR OF NATURAL LAW (Samuel Rachel), and two years later the university of LUND elected SAMUEL PUFENDORF to a new chair of natural and international law. His most important work is DE JURE NATURAE ET GENTIUM (1672), summarised in DE OFFICIO HOMINIS ET CIVIS (1673) — and the latter was enormously popular: NEARLY A HUNDRED EDITIONS IN THE COURSE OF A CENTURY, including translations into German, French, English, Danish, Dutch, Italian and Russian. It is no exaggeration to say that EVERY EDUCATED MAN AND MANY WOMEN IN EUROPE READ IT. The method owes far more to MATHEMATICS than to the moral theology that preceded Grotius: in the ELEMENTA JURISPRUDENTIAE NATURALIS he sets out TWENTY-ONE DEFINITIONS, TWO AXIOMS AND FIVE OBSERVATIONS, on the model of his teacher, the Jena professor of mathematics ERHARD WEIGEL (whose 'Arithmetical Description of Moral Wisdom' of 1674 says so in its title). In the same spirit LEIBNIZ published his mathematically flavoured NOVA METHODUS in 1667. The relation between THE UNQUESTIONABLE OBJECTIVITY OF MATHEMATICAL TRUTH AND THE LESS OBVIOUS OBJECTIVITY OF MORAL TRUTH is here entirely clear.

cards.q: When was the first chair of natural law created and who was the most influential author?
cards.a: In 1665 at KIEL (Samuel Rachel); two years later LUND elected SAMUEL PUFENDORF to a new chair of natural and international law. His De Officio Hominis et Civis (1673) went through nearly a hundred editions in a century and was translated into seven languages — practically every educated European read it.

cards.q: How does Pufendorf's method differ from what preceded Grotius?
cards.a: It owes far more to MATHEMATICS than to moral theology: the Elementa sets out 21 definitions, 2 axioms and 5 observations, on the model of the mathematician Erhard Weigel. It is the transfer of the unquestionable objectivity of mathematical truth to the less obvious objectivity of moral truth.

cards.q: What does Pufendorf start from and what does he derive from it?
cards.a: From the SOCIABILITY OF MAN, like Grotius, and he derives from it ever more concrete rules divided into DUTIES TOWARDS GOD, TOWARDS ONE'S NEIGHBOUR AND TOWARDS ONESELF. His approach is secular in that it does not depend on the doctrines of any revealed religion — though the binding force ultimately flows from a divine command.

11.title: Why it captivated the lawyers
11.text: From a legal point of view the main thing is this: PUFENDORF (and to a lesser extent Grotius) GAVE NATURAL LAW A RATIONAL STRUCTURE. That, together with an APPARENT MORAL OBJECTIVITY, allowed it to serve as a MODEL FOR POSITIVE LEGAL ORDERS. And for the continental systems with a substantial Roman law component there was a further attraction: THE EXTENT TO WHICH THE CONCRETE RULES DESIGNATED BY PUFENDORF AS NATURAL LAW OVERLAPPED WITH THE RULES OF ROMAN LAW. At the beginning of the 18th century natural law formed the mainstream of political philosophy and ethics, and the main difference between theories lay in WHICH PRINCIPLES THEY TOOK AS THEIR FOUNDATION. In England HOBBES stood between Grotius and Pufendorf — influenced by the first, influential on the second, but with quite different starting points — and LOCKE recommended both for their educational value. Through GERSHOM CARMICHAEL natural law lay at the roots of the SCOTTISH ENLIGHTENMENT. In Germany CHRISTIAN THOMASIUS, 'the father of the German Enlightenment', BROKE THE BOND BETWEEN NATURAL AND ROMAN LAW and argued that NATURAL LAW IS NOTHING MORE THAN AN IDEAL MODEL FOR POSITIVE LAWS AND HAS NO BINDING DIMENSION OF ITS OWN. CHRISTIAN WOLFF, from 1740 in the chair of natural law, international law and mathematics at HALLE, wrote the eight-volume JUS NATURAE METHODO SCIENTIFICA PERTRACTATUM — he tried the 'scientific method' on economics, psychology and cosmology too. In Switzerland BURLAMAQUI wrote the Principles of Natural and Politic Law, which INFLUENCED THE FOUNDING FATHERS OF THE USA. And JEAN BARBEYRAC, a Frenchman teaching in Switzerland, Germany and Holland, prepared editions of Grotius and Pufendorf with copious notes of his own. ONLY AT THE END OF THE 18TH CENTURY DID THE DOMINANCE OF NATURAL LAW THINKING BEGIN TO WANE — most markedly and most influentially in the work of KANT.

cards.q: Why was natural law so attractive to lawyers?
cards.a: Because Pufendorf (and to a lesser extent Grotius) gave it a RATIONAL STRUCTURE which, together with an apparent moral objectivity, allowed it to be used as a MODEL for positive legal orders. The continental systems with a Roman law component were further attracted by the extent to which Pufendorf's 'natural' rules OVERLAPPED WITH ROMAN LAW.

cards.q: What did Christian Thomasius do to natural law?
cards.a: The 'father of the German Enlightenment' BROKE THE BOND BETWEEN NATURAL AND ROMAN LAW and argued that natural law is nothing more than an IDEAL MODEL for positive laws and HAS NO BINDING DIMENSION OF ITS OWN — while, like most people in the 18th century, undoubtedly believing in God and even writing a volume on the foundations of divine law.

12.title: Where the method fails: the case of mandate
12.text: Ibbetson's sharpest passage, and the best critical card in the whole article. Pufendorf concluded that under natural law A MAN MUST TAKE REASONABLE CARE NOT TO CAUSE ANOTHER HARM, and also that HE MUST PERFORM HIS AGREEMENTS. These principles evidently collide over the question of WHAT DEGREE OF CARE A CONTRACTING PARTY OWES IN PERFORMING A MANDATE — that is, an agreed act performed GRATUITOUSLY for another. Roman law was said to have a rule that the mandatary must show THE HIGHEST CARE, EXACTISSIMA DILIGENTIA (although Barbeyrac noted that there are several Roman texts and they contradict one another). Pufendorf preferred the view that THE DEGREE OF CARE SHOULD BE THAT WHICH THE MANDATARY GENERALLY SHOWS IN HIS OWN AFFAIRS. And Ibbetson calls it what it is: IT WAS A MERE ASSERTION, DERIVABLE FROM NEITHER OF THE GENERAL PROPOSITIONS from which it was supposed to follow. As Barbeyrac pointed out, different natural lawyers took different positions — and ALL OF THEM EVIDENTLY RESTED ON INTUITIONS AT THE LEVEL OF DETAIL, NOT ON DEDUCTION FROM MORE GENERAL PRINCIPLES. And the generalisation: HOWEVER IT LOOKED, THE TRANSITIONS FROM MORE GENERAL TO MORE CONCRETE PROPOSITIONS WERE NOT DEDUCTIONS IN THE MATHEMATICAL SENSE OF NECESSARY CONCLUSIONS FROM PREMISES. They might be PLAUSIBLE, but no more. Even a reader who accepted the starting point of the chain could disagree with almost any step at almost any point. THE APPEARANCE OF OBJECTIVITY WAS WHOLLY SUPERFICIAL.

cards.q: On what example does Ibbetson show the failure of the natural law method?
cards.a: On the degree of care in MANDATE — a gratuitous agreed act for another. Pufendorf's principles (do no harm, perform agreements) collide here, and his solution — the care the mandatary shows in his own affairs — was A MERE ASSERTION, derivable from neither. Barbeyrac showed that different authors reached different conclusions, all resting on intuitions at the level of detail.

cards.q: How does Ibbetson assess the 'deductions' of the natural lawyers in general?
cards.a: That they were NOT deductions in the mathematical sense of necessary conclusions from premises. They might be plausible, but no more: even a reader who accepted the starting point could disagree with almost any step at almost any point. THE APPEARANCE OF OBJECTIVITY WAS WHOLLY SUPERFICIAL.

13.title: Domat: natural law as mere arrangement
13.text: The Frenchman JEAN DOMAT went another way. France had no tradition of studying natural law at the universities, but it is probable (if not documented) that he knew the main 17th-century authors. In LES LOIX CIVILES DANS LEUR ORDRE NATUREL (1693) he ACCEPTED ROMAN LAW AS IT STOOD IN THE CORPUS JURIS CIVILIS BUT REARRANGED ITS TEXTS ACCORDING TO WHAT HE TOOK TO BE THEIR RATIONAL BASIS. Since Roman law then formed the basis of French law (with customary deviations), HE DID NOT HAVE TO WORRY ABOUT THE VALIDITY OF THE RULES OR THEIR DERIVATION FROM FIRST PRINCIPLES — although it is clear from the preface that he accepted the premises of the natural lawyers of his day and believed that Roman law for the most part embodies natural law. NATURAL LAW THEREFORE GAVE THE CONTENT OF THE WORK ONLY A RATIONAL STRUCTURE intended to make Roman law easier to grasp. And Ibbetson's sober note: THERE WAS NOTHING MAGICAL ABOUT THAT ARRANGEMENT and other arrangements existed which made the Roman scheme more intelligible — POTHIER rearranged the Digest differently in his PANDECTAE JUSTINIANAE, and other French works, such as Serres's Institutions du Droit François, went on keeping the order of Justinian's Institutes. The Englishman SIR WILLIAM JONES put the whole thing best: 'IF LAW BE A SCIENCE, AND REALLY DESERVE SO SUBLIME A NAME, IT MUST BE FOUNDED ON PRINCIPLE AND CLAIM AN EXALTED RANK IN THE EMPIRE OF REASON; BUT IF IT BE MERELY AN UNCONNECTED SERIES OF DECREES AND ORDINANCES, ITS USE MAY REMAIN, THOUGH ITS DIGNITY BE LESSENED — AND HE WILL BECOME THE GREATEST LAWYER WHO HAS THE STRONGEST MEMORY.'

cards.q: What does natural law do in Domat's work?
cards.a: It supplies only a RATIONAL STRUCTURE. Domat accepted Roman law as it stood in the Corpus Juris Civilis and merely rearranged its texts according to their supposed rational basis — because Roman law was in force in France he did not have to address the validity of the rules or their derivation from first principles.

cards.q: Why was a rational arrangement of law sought at all? Quote Jones.
cards.a: 'If law be a science, and really deserve so sublime a name, it must be founded on principle and claim an exalted rank in the empire of reason; but if it be merely an unconnected series of decrees and ordinances, its use may remain, though its dignity be lessened — and he will become the greatest lawyer who has the strongest memory.'

14.title: Ius naturale and ius gentium: three lines
14.text: It is often said that Grotius is the father of international law — but the tradition can be traced A HUNDRED YEARS BEFORE HIM, to FRANCISCO DE VITORIA (whom Grotius acknowledges) and DOMINGO DE SOTO. Vitoria and Soto were concerned with THE JUSTIFICATION, OR LACK OF JUSTIFICATION, OF SPANISH IMPERIAL RULE IN THE AMERICAS; natural law arguments were used here to DEFINE THE EXTENT OF THE SPANISH KING'S POWER — and Vitoria also used them to support the conclusion that CHRISTIANS MAY IN APPROPRIATE CIRCUMSTANCES LAWFULLY WAGE WAR. The break at Grotius is therefore not one of originality or rigour, but that HE BROKE THE BOND WITH CATHOLIC THEOLOGY AND WROTE AT A MANAGEABLE LENGTH. A few years before De Jure Belli ac Pacis, moreover, FRANCISCO SUÁREZ firmly distinguished IUS NATURALE from IUS GENTIUM: the latter applies ONLY TO RELATIONS BETWEEN STATES (unlike natural law, which applies between individuals too) and flows from AN EXPRESS OR TACIT AGREEMENT AMONG THEM (unlike natural law, which flows from the nature of man). In the following century THREE LINES can be distinguished: PUFENDORF'S, for which ius naturale and universally valid ius gentium are INDISTINGUISHABLE, so that interstate relations are governed by unchanging principles unless supplemented by particular treaties; the line of RACHEL AND TEXTOR, which draws A SHARP LINE between them while acknowledging that natural law forms an important part of the law governing interstate relations; and the PRAGMATIC line, which looks to THE ACTUAL PRACTICE OF STATES. BY THE MIDDLE OF THE 18TH CENTURY THE PURELY NATURAL LAW LINE HAD EXHAUSTED ITSELF: WOLFF published his Jus Gentium alongside his Jus Naturae, symbolically separating the two, and in 1758 VATTEL published his DROIT DES GENS IN THE VERNACULAR rather than in learned Latin — he did not exclude natural law, but after Grotius laid greater weight on the VOLUNTARY side of interstate relations.

terms.def: Ius gentium applies only between states and flows from their express or tacit agreement; ius naturale applies between individuals too and flows from the nature of man.

cards.q: How did Suárez distinguish ius naturale from ius gentium?
cards.a: Ius gentium applies ONLY to relations between states and flows from their EXPRESS OR TACIT AGREEMENT; ius naturale applies between individuals too and flows from THE NATURE OF MAN. Grotius took the distinction over, though he uses it rather ambiguously throughout his work.

cards.q: Name the three lines in the history of international law after Grotius.
cards.a: Pufendorf's, for which ius naturale and general ius gentium are indistinguishable, so that interstate relations are governed by unchanging principles unless supplemented by treaties; Rachel's and Textor's, which draws a sharp line between them; and the PRAGMATIC line, looking to the actual practice of states. By the mid-18th century the purely natural law line had exhausted itself.

cards.q: Why is Grotius a break, when Vitoria and Soto came a century before him?
cards.a: Not for originality or rigour. Vitoria and Soto were concerned with justifying Spanish rule in the Americas, and natural law defined for them the extent of the king's power. Grotius's break lies in his HAVING BROKEN THE BOND WITH CATHOLIC THEOLOGY and written at a manageable length.

15.title: What all the versions had in common
15.text: A summary before the codifications, and the best single card from the article. Between Grotius and Wolff many versions of natural law arose, but they had several FEATURES IN COMMON. Already from the generation BEFORE Grotius they were CUT LOOSE FROM DEPENDENCE ON THE WILL OF GOD — as Grotius memorably put it, THEY WOULD HOLD EVEN IF GOD DID NOT EXIST. God was not wholly irrelevant: the BINDING FORCE of natural law flowed from his command to do good and abstain from evil, BUT THE DETERMINATION OF ITS PRECEPTS OWED HIM NOTHING. The formulation of concrete rules was THE WORK OF HUMAN REASON, proceeding from a few very basic premises which could be taken as self-evident. That CENTRALITY OF REASON was entirely in accord with Enlightenment thought: JUST AS SCIENTIFIC TRUTHS ARE TRUE IN THEMSELVES, SO ARE THE MORAL TRUTHS IN NATURAL LAW TRUE IN THEMSELVES. It was precisely this that allowed them to keep the UNCHANGEABILITY which was at the core of Aristotelian and Stoic thought. And above all: whereas pre-Grotian writings concentrated on the FUNDAMENTAL NATURE of natural law, FROM GROTIUS ONWARDS THEY CONCENTRATE ON ITS CONCRETE CONTENT — and that content moreover appeared ORDERED, and therefore in principle INTELLIGIBLE TO ANYONE.

cards.q: What did all the versions of natural law between Grotius and Wolff have in common?
cards.a: They were cut loose from dependence on the will of God (binding force from a divine command, yes, but not the DETERMINATION of the content); the concrete rules were the work of HUMAN REASON from a few self-evident premises; that centrality of reason matched the Enlightenment — moral truths are true in themselves like scientific ones; and from Grotius attention shifted from the NATURE of natural law to its CONCRETE CONTENT, which appeared ordered and therefore intelligible to anyone.

16.title: Montesquieu: a variable natural law
16.text: A complement was MONTESQUIEU's theory in L'ESPRIT DES LOIS (1743). Whether to count him among the natural lawyers is largely a matter of terminology: HE DID NOT BELIEVE THERE WAS A FIXED, UNCHANGING BODY OF LAWS, DERIVABLE BY REASON, VALID FOR ALL NATIONS ALIKE. He argued instead that the law appropriate to any nation depends on its POLITICAL CONSTITUTION (actual or desirable), on ITS HISTORY, SOCIAL STRUCTURE, GEOGRAPHY AND CLIMATE. This can be taken as A FORM OF VARIABLE NATURAL LAW, adaptable to the circumstances of each nation. And this is the key connection: IT WAS PRECISELY MONTESQUIEU'S THEORY, ENJOINING THE ADAPTATION OF LAWS TO THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF INDIVIDUAL NATIONS, THAT ALLOWED NATURAL LAW THINKING TO TAKE HOLD IN THE ABSOLUTIST MONARCHIES of continental Europe. It can be seen in the INSTRUCTIONS OF CATHERINE THE GREAT to the legislative commission of 1767: 'THOSE LAWS HAVE THE GREATEST CONFORMITY WITH NATURE WHOSE PARTICULAR PROVISIONS ARE BEST ADAPTED TO THE SITUATION AND CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE PEOPLE FOR WHOM THEY ARE MADE.'

cards.q: Why is Montesquieu the key to how natural law took hold in the absolutist monarchies?
cards.a: Because he did not believe in a fixed, unchanging body of laws valid for all nations, but in law adapted to the political constitution, history, social structure, geography and climate — a kind of VARIABLE natural law. That allowed rulers to codify 'according to natural reason' and yet according to their own circumstances; it can be seen in Catherine the Great's Instructions of 1767.

17.title: Codification I: the Prussian attempts and what they really were
17.text: The roots of the codification movement lie in the 17th century, but the works of that time were LITTLE MORE THAN COLLECTIONS OF THE LAW IN FORCE. The whole movement changed in the middle of the 18th century. The trigger was the ORDERS OF FREDERICK WILLIAM I OF PRUSSIA IN 1713 AND 1714 to unify the various laws of his territories: the law was to be codified 'ACCORDING TO REASON' and the supervision was entrusted to the natural lawyer CHRISTIAN THOMASIUS. The draft came to nothing, but here already one can see what role natural law might play. A further order, that of FREDERICK THE GREAT IN 1746, this time to SAMUEL COCCEJI, demanded that the law be INTELLIGIBLE and codified ON THE BASIS OF NATURAL REASON AND THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE TERRITORY — natural law thinking is visible here both in the reference to reason and in the person of Cocceji, but THE RESULTING DRAFT OWED MORE TO DOMAT'S STRUCTURAL CONCERNS THAN TO WOLFF'S SUBSTANTIVE ONES. And the sober summary worth remembering: that draft and the criminal and civil codes issued in BAVARIA IN 1751 AND 1753 WERE ESSENTIALLY CODES OF ROMAN LAW, AN EXPANDED VERSION OF JUSTINIAN'S INSTITUTES. Codification projects were also brought forward in the second half of the century by BADEN, HANOVER, HESSE-DARMSTADT, HESSE-KASSEL, MECKLENBURG AND SAXONY — and in 1766 AUSTRIA began a half-century process that issued in the CODE OF 1811.

cards.q: How did the codifications of the mid-18th century differ from those of the 17th, and how did they not?
cards.a: The older works were little more than COLLECTIONS OF THE LAW IN FORCE; the new ones were to be codified 'according to reason' (Frederick William I 1713/14, Frederick the Great 1746). In practice, however, the resulting drafts and the Bavarian codes of 1751 and 1753 were essentially CODES OF ROMAN LAW, an expanded version of Justinian's Institutes — and owed more to Domat's arrangement than to Wolff's substance.

18.title: Codification II: the Prussian ALR 1794 and why it is not yet a natural law code
18.text: The first great Prussian codification and the first successful attempt at a code that is more than a collection of rules in force came in 1794: the ALLGEMEINES LANDRECHT. It rested on Roman law, which was formally in force (in its 18th-century shape), but THIS WAS EXPLAINED BY THE FACT THAT ROMAN LAW IS LARGELY FOUNDED ON NATURAL REASON. The draft was moreover widely circulated for comment, among others to PROFESSORS OF NATURAL LAW at the universities, so that the final version contains elements strongly reminiscent of WOLFF, most markedly in its assumption about THE ROLE OF LEGISLATION IN SOCIETY. And yet — and here is the distinguishing question — IT WAS HARDLY A 'NATURAL LAW CODE' IN THE FULL SENSE. Natural law was there in the structure and in some particular provisions, but the code consisted of AN ENORMOUS NUMBER OF PROVISIONS, AROUND 20,000, and it lacked the SIMPLICITY OF LANGUAGE that would have made it generally intelligible, and the ABSTRACTION that would have enabled citizens and judges to apply it to new cases as they arose.

cards.q: Why is the Prussian ALR of 1794 hardly a 'natural law code' in the full sense?
cards.a: Because it had around 20,000 PROVISIONS and lacked the SIMPLICITY of language that would have made it generally intelligible and the ABSTRACTION that would have let judges and citizens apply it to new cases. Natural law was in it only in the structure and in part of the provisions — and the Roman law on which it rested was justified by the claim that Roman law is itself founded on natural reason.

19.title: Codification III: the Code civil as the first true natural law code
19.text: After Domat, attempts to make the law more intelligible multiplied in France; the most important was FRANÇOIS BOURJON, LE DROIT COMMUN DE FRANCE (1747), which may be regarded as THE FIRST REAL STEP TOWARDS THE CODIFICATION OF FRENCH LAW — his real concern was THE REARRANGEMENT OF THE LAW INTO A RATIONAL AND INTELLIGIBLE FORM. POTHIER followed, and JEAN DE DIEU D'OLIVIER, and all of this issued in the CODE CIVIL. After the revolution several drafts were produced, until the NAPOLEONIC CODE CIVIL of 1804 arrived, supplemented by a criminal code, codes of civil and criminal procedure, a commercial and a military code — but it was the CODE CIVIL that showed the greatest reliance on natural law. Its structure owed much to Bourjon, its content clearly to Domat and Pothier. And the decisive difference from the Prussian code of 1794: IT WAS BUILT ON ABSTRACT PROPOSITIONS AND THEREFORE HAD THE CAPACITY TO REACH NEW AND UNFORESEEN SITUATIONS. In that sense it may be regarded as the FIRST TRUE 'NATURAL LAW CODE'. Its foundation is stated transparently in the opening sentence of PORTALIS'S preamble: 'THERE EXISTS A UNIVERSAL AND UNCHANGING LAW, THE SOURCE OF ALL POSITIVE LAWS; IT IS NOTHING OTHER THAN NATURAL REASON IN SO FAR AS IT GOVERNS ALL MEN.'

cards.q: Why is the Code civil the first true 'natural law code'?
cards.a: Because unlike the Prussian ALR it was built on ABSTRACT PROPOSITIONS and therefore had the capacity to reach new and unforeseen situations. Its structure owed to Bourjon, its content to Domat and Pothier, and its foundation is stated by Portalis's preamble: 'There exists a universal and unchanging law, the source of all positive laws; it is nothing other than natural reason in so far as it governs all men.'

20.title: From duties to rights
20.text: At that period, however, the centre of gravity of natural law was SHIFTING. Montesquieu's influence was unmistakable and allowed a legal text TO BE ADAPTED TO ITS PARTICULAR CIRCUMSTANCES. And secondly: WHEREAS GROTIUS, PUFENDORF AND THEIR FOLLOWERS WERE CONCERNED ABOVE ALL WITH THE DUTIES NATURAL LAW CREATES, AT THE END OF THE 18TH CENTURY MORE ATTENTION WAS PAID TO THE INDIVIDUAL RIGHTS NATURAL LAW CREATES. Natural law thereby came into accord with the INDIVIDUALIST AND EGALITARIAN SPIRIT of revolutionary France, most clearly in the DECLARATION OF THE RIGHTS OF MAN AND OF THE CITIZEN OF 1789 — JUST AS IT HAD EARLIER BEEN ADAPTABLE TO MONARCHICAL ABSOLUTISM. That is the sentence worth being able to produce: the same doctrine served Catherine the Great and the Declaration alike, because it could be shaped.

cards.q: What shift occurred in natural law at the end of the 18th century?
cards.a: From the DUTIES natural law creates (Grotius, Pufendorf) to the INDIVIDUAL RIGHTS it creates. It thereby came into accord with the individualist and egalitarian spirit of revolutionary France — most clearly in the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789 — just as it had earlier been adaptable to monarchical absolutism.

21.title: The ABGB 1811: the last of the original natural law codes
21.text: The last of the original natural law codes is the Austrian ABGB OF 1811, drafted by a commission headed by FRANZ VON ZEILLER, who had studied under ANTON VON MARTINI, the leading Austrian natural lawyer of the second half of the 18th century, and was rector of the University of Vienna. Martini's influence was evident, but so was KANT'S, which led to an emphasis on INDIVIDUAL FREEDOM. And now the balance that is valued in an exam: AS SUITED THE POLITICAL SITUATION IN AUSTRIA, THE ABGB HAD MORE IN COMMON WITH THE PRUSSIAN CIVIL CODE OF 1794 THAN WITH THE INDIVIDUALIST CODE CIVIL: it took over the idea of individual freedom on the basis that A STRUCTURE OF RIGHTS AND DUTIES IS NEEDED IF CITIZENS ARE TO EXERCISE THEIR FREEDOM. But like its French predecessor it was formulated AT A LEVEL OF ABSTRACTION that allowed it to be adapted to changing needs. Zeiller himself wrote an introduction to the ABGB in which he stressed its FUNDAMENTAL DEPENDENCE ON NATURAL LAW. The year 1811 is the end of the MAKING of new natural law codes, NOT the end of natural law codes: the French and Austrian civil codes became the basis of many others in Europe and beyond, with the French increasingly predominant by the middle of the 19th century.

cards.q: Which is the ABGB closer to — the Prussian ALR or the Code civil, and why?
cards.a: The PRUSSIAN ALR, as suited the political situation in Austria. It took over the idea of individual freedom (Kant's influence through Zeiller, who studied under Martini) on the basis that A STRUCTURE OF RIGHTS AND DUTIES IS NEEDED IF CITIZENS ARE TO EXERCISE THEIR FREEDOM. What it shares with the Code civil is its LEVEL OF ABSTRACTION, which allowed adaptation to changing needs.

cards.q: What ends in 1811 and what does not?
cards.a: The MAKING of new natural law codes ends, not the natural law codes themselves: the French and Austrian civil codes became the basis of many others in Europe and beyond, the French predominating by the middle of the 19th century.

cards.q: Why did belief in natural law die out?
cards.a: Because LAW CAME INCREASINGLY TO BE UNDERSTOOD AS A HUMAN CREATION IN WHICH THE QUALITY OF RULES DEPENDS ON THEIR SOCIAL EFFECTS AND NOT ON THEIR SUPPOSEDLY RATIONAL FOUNDATION. Reliance on natural law exhausted itself, while the codes founded on it remained.

22.title: England: two differences
22.text: The role of natural law in England was ATYPICAL FOR TWO REASONS. First: UNLIKE THE CONTINENTAL SYSTEMS, BUILT AROUND THE INSTITUTIONAL SCHEME OF ROMAN LAW, THE ENGLISH COMMON LAW HAD NO ABSTRACT FRAMEWORK TO LEAN ON BEFORE THE 18TH CENTURY. Second: THERE WAS NO CODIFICATION MOVEMENT corresponding to the continental one, so that when the influence of natural law thinking began to show, IT HAD TO BE FITTED INTO EXISTING LAW OR LAID OVER IT FROM ABOVE. In the second half of the 15th century the idea of natural law was widespread in English law BUT VERY THIN. Where any theory is visible it is wholly orthodox: natural law is given by God and human understanding recognises it as existing — so the exposition of the law of reason in CHRISTOPHER ST GERMAN's DOCTOR AND STUDENT has it. Isolated mentions continue in the 16th and early 17th centuries, all in accord with Doctor and Student — except perhaps the line associated with CHIEF JUSTICE SIR EDWARD COKE, who inclined to IDENTIFYING THE COMMON LAW ITSELF WITH THE LAW OF NATURE. FROM 1640 the influence of Grotius's De Jure Belli ac Pacis began to show, as legal argument came to refer to the law of nature.

cards.q: Why was the role of natural law in England atypical?
cards.a: For two reasons: the common law had NO ABSTRACT FRAMEWORK to lean on before the 18th century (unlike continental systems built around the institutional scheme of Roman law), and there was NO CODIFICATION MOVEMENT — so natural law thinking had to be fitted into existing law or laid over it from above.

23.title: England: where natural law actually flowed through
23.text: The influence went much further than contentless declarations that natural law (or the law of God) is part of the law of England. Not every lawyer was enthusiastic — in 1670 CHIEF JUSTICE VAUGHAN criticised the way such arguments were used: 'AS THE LAW OF NATURE IS COMMONLY SPOKEN OF, IT IS THE PONS STULTORUM — THE BRIDGE OF FOOLS; WHEN FOOLS KNOW NOT THEIR WAY, THEY GO THAT WAY.' Even so, the findings of the natural lawyers settled into English law, and most clearly in CONTRACT LAW. The first treatise on it, by SIR JEFFREY GILBERT at the beginning of the 18th century, shows the clear influence of HOBBES and probably of LOCKE, and Hobbes's model of contract lay fairly plainly behind the law of set-off. The first published work on the subject, the TREATISE ON EQUITY attributed to HENRY BALLOW (1737), took ALL BUT ONE OF ITS CHAPTER HEADINGS FROM UNACKNOWLEDGED QUOTATIONS from the English translation of Pufendorf. More significant still were POTHIER'S works, introduced into England in the 1780s, which at the beginning of the 19th century shaped EVERY ASPECT OF ENGLISH CONTRACT LAW. And not only contract: in TORT the idea of NEGLIGENCE, which came to dominate modern law, first appeared in FRANCIS BULLER (1767), derived directly or indirectly FROM PUFENDORF; the understanding of the TRUST at the beginning of the 18th century also appears to have rested on the English translation of Pufendorf. In the early rules of COPYRIGHT, by contrast, natural law arguments were REJECTED. Summary: the natural lawyers' arguments were used in the English courts ROUTINELY, with the English translation of Pufendorf the dominant influence, BUT THIS WAS NOT A WHOLESALE RECEPTION — arguments founded on them might succeed or fail.

terms.def: 'The bridge of fools' — Vaughan's 1670 jibe at arguments from the law of nature: when men know not their way, they go that way.

cards.q: Where did natural law actually flow into English law?
cards.a: Chiefly through CONTRACT LAW: Gilbert's treatise under the influence of Hobbes and Locke, Ballow's Treatise on Equity (1737), which took almost all its chapter headings from the English translation of Pufendorf, and from the 1780s Pothier, who shaped every aspect of contract law. Also NEGLIGENCE in tort (Buller 1767, from Pufendorf) and the understanding of the trust. In copyright, by contrast, natural law arguments were rejected.

cards.q: What does Vaughan's 'pons stultorum' mean?
cards.a: 'The bridge of fools' — his criticism of 1670 of how arguments from the law of nature are commonly used: when fools know not their way, they go that way. A reminder that an argument from natural law is often a substitute for an argument.

24.title: Blackstone and the deepest influence of all
24.text: It is not surprising that references to Grotius and Pufendorf are found in the most important English legal work of the 18th century, BLACKSTONE'S COMMENTARIES (1765–9); nor should it surprise us that they are rather HAPHAZARD, introduced where they seemed useful and not in any systematic way. Blackstone's declared intention TO RELATE ENGLISH LAW TO THE LAW OF NATURE fits into Europe-wide 18th-century thought. The Commentaries are certainly not a natural law work in which ever more concrete precepts are built on foundations of self-evident propositions — but the influence of natural law on their thinking is marked: UNLIKE THE FOUR VOLUMES OF COKE'S INSTITUTES of the first half of the 17th century, Blackstone's analysis has a SYSTEMATIC STRUCTURE, pointing to law having a foundation in reasonableness. This way of thinking generated a mass of legal treatises, in the early ones of which natural law is transparently present and which built further on this rational approach. And in conclusion THE DEEPEST INFLUENCE OF ALL, which goes beyond Blackstone: IT WAS PRECISELY THIS WAY OF THINKING ABOUT LAW. The common law's focus on the FORMS OF ACTION and equity's focus on HIGHLY TECHNICAL RULES was muted as the technical rules of both systems were squeezed into a RATIONAL, ABSTRACT FRAMEWORK. And then the point: THE RULES OF THE SYSTEM WERE NO LONGER MERELY THE RULES OF THE SYSTEM; THEY WERE SUFFUSED WITH A MORAL QUALITY THAT GAVE THEM A JUSTIFICATION BEYOND THE FACT THAT THEY WERE THE LAW.

cards.q: What was the deepest influence of natural law on English law?
cards.a: Not the reception of concrete rules but the WAY OF THINKING ABOUT LAW: the common law's focus on the forms of action and equity's on technical rules was muted as both were squeezed into a rational, abstract framework. The rules of the system were no longer merely the rules of the system — they were suffused with a MORAL QUALITY giving them a justification beyond the fact that they were the law.

cards.q: How do Blackstone's Commentaries differ from Coke's Institutes?
cards.a: By a systematic STRUCTURE pointing to law having a foundation in reasonableness — which Coke's Institutes of the first half of the 17th century lack. Blackstone's references to Grotius and Pufendorf are, however, haphazard, and the Commentaries are not a natural law work.
